title: First-Principles Atomistic Structure and Dynamics of Polyethylene During High-Pressure Radical Polymerization via Machine Learning Force Fields
authors: Bharatha K. Gunawardana, Teresa Shah, Bicha Azizova, Deepa Ranabhat, Yizhi Song, Akshath Shastri, Srinjoy Ghose, Thomas E. Gartner, Hsin-Yu Ko
abstract: Polyethylene (PE) is one of the most commonly used synthetic polymers. While the synthesis and processing protocols for PE are well established, precise experimental assignment of microscopic structures at atomistic resolution (i.e., the position of each atom) remains largely limited to highly crystalline systems. This gap is often addressed via computer simulations using empirical interatomic potentials, which use approximate but efficient descriptions of interatomic interactions to reach the length and time scales needed to describe macromolecules. These empirical potentials typically perform well for bulk and/or collective properties but face challenges with chemical realism for complex systems, e.g., during reactive processes. In this work, we address this challenge by combining the computational efficiency of a deep potential (DP) machine-learning force field and the chemical realism of first-principles van der Waals (vdW) corrected hybrid density functional theory (DFT) enabled by a SeA high-throughput framework. Using this approach, we study the structure and dynamics of PE oligomers and polymers in an ethylene solvent under common high-pressure (supercritical) radical polymerization conditions. We found that the local solvation environment of radical-containing PE oligomers converges for chain lengths greater than (n~6), suggesting extensibility of our oligomer-trained MLFF to significantly longer polymers. We then confirmed the extensibility of these models to long PE chains by characterizing the molecular weight scaling of single-chain structure and dynamics, which showed classic good solvent behavior. Our PE MLFF retained a consistent level of fidelity and stability across a wide range of thermodynamic state points and chain lengths, at full atomistic resolution, therefore paving the way towards first-principles-based polymer structure and property prediction.
summary: This work addresses the limitation of simulating polymer structure at the atomic level under reactive conditions by developing a Deep Potential Machine Learning Force Field (MLFF). The MLFF is trained using high-accuracy DFT data and is successfully applied to model Polyethylene polymerization. This demonstrates a powerful, first-principles approach for predicting polymer properties across large length and time scales.
main_problem: The primary challenge is accurately simulating the atomistic structure and dynamics of polymers like Polyethylene (PE) under reactive, high-pressure conditions, a task difficult for traditional empirical potentials.
main_result: The authors successfully developed and validated a Deep Potential Machine Learning Force Field (MLFF) that accurately predicts PE structure and dynamics across various thermodynamic states and chain lengths, demonstrating first-principles accuracy for polymer simulation.
method: The methodology combines the computational efficiency of a Deep Potential MLFF with the high chemical accuracy of first-principles, van der Waals corrected hybrid Density Functional Theory (DFT), facilitated by a high-throughput framework.
model_or_system: The system studied is Polyethylene (PE) oligomers and polymers undergoing radical polymerization in an ethylene solvent under supercritical, high-pressure conditions. The model is the MLFF trained on DFT data, enabling large-scale Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulations.
key_observables: Local solvation environment (via RDFs), molecular weight scaling of structure/dynamics, and consistent fidelity across varying thermodynamic state points.
important_parameters: High-pressure/supercritical conditions ($p \ge 500 	ext{ bar}$), temperature range ($200-600 	ext{ K}$), and oligomer chain lengths ($n=1$ to $n=6$).
main_assumptions: The MLFF trained on oligomers can be reliably extrapolated to predict the behavior of significantly longer, full-length polymer chains.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the MLFF training workflow using SeA and the DP ecosystem, and show structural convergence of the solvation environment around radical-containing oligomers.
paper_structure: The paper details the necessity of bridging the gap between DFT accuracy and large-scale simulation needs. It outlines the MLFF training process using high-throughput DFT data, validates the model by studying oligomer solvation structures, and finally demonstrates the model's extensibility to long polymer chains.
why_interesting: The use of MLFFs trained on high-level quantum chemistry methods to model complex, reactive condensed matter systems is highly relevant for developing predictive tools in quantum materials and soft matter physics.
